title: How Hot Wheels Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss Hot Wheels: the toy die-cast car line's origins in 1968 as a rival to Matchbox, designer Harry Bradley and the first sixteen cars (including the Camaro and the pre-release Corvette), the Spectraflame paint and red line tires, the move from Hawthorne, California to Hong Kong and later Malaysia, Saturday morning cartoon and fast food Happy Meal promotions (including the 1983 citation), the Treasure Hunt series, collector values (Beach Bomb, Cheetah/Python, diamond-studded anniversary car), scale design and fantasy cars, and the die-cast manufacturing process. The episode closes with a listener mail proposal from Joe Prohaska in Reno, Nevada about tying the minimum wage to a living-wage standard.

segments.title: Opening banter and childhood Hot Wheels memories
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the opening and reminisce about childhood toys, including Hot Wheels, G.I. Joe, and a book report visual aid.

segments.title: Hot Wheels as the largest vehicle maker by count
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh note that more than four billion Hot Wheels have been produced, more than the big four Detroit automakers combined, and speculate about tire counts.

segments.title: Origins: Elliott Handler, Matchbox rivalry and Harry Bradley
segments.summary: Mattel's Elliott Handler enters the die-cast market dominated by Tyco's Matchbox cars. The name is linked to a Harry Bradley hot rod and the original commercials' pronunciation.

segments.title: First sixteen cars and early engineering
segments.summary: The first sixteen Hot Wheels released in 1968 at 59 cents each, designed by Harry Bradley, including a Camaro and a Corvette released before the real 1969 model. Early cars had working suspension, red line tires, and Spectraflame paint, and were built to race and beat Matchbox.

segments.title: Production move overseas, cartoon, and Happy Meals
segments.summary: Production moved from Hawthorne, California to Hong Kong, and features were downgraded. A 1970 Saturday morning cartoon followed, and fast food promotions including a 1983 McDonald's Happy Meal set with the Citation.

segments.title: Treasure Hunt series, collecting and most valuable cars
segments.summary: The limited Treasure Hunt series was introduced and then widened. The Beach Bomb, a pink VW bus, is described as the most valuable, and the Cheetah/Python name change adds value. A diamond-studded 2008 anniversary car is also mentioned.

segments.title: Design, scale, fantasy cars, and die-cast manufacturing
segments.summary: Designers once measured real cars by hand and now use computer design and 3D printing. Hot Wheels widen wheel wells for looks, include fantasy cars, and are die-cast from molds. Mainline cars cost about a dollar.

segments.title: Collecting, museum exhibit and off-topic chat
segments.summary: Discussion of a Peterson Automotive Museum exhibit with full-size Hot Wheels cars, the first Hot Wheels convention in Toledo, Ohio, and an unrelated conversation about Mad Max, Vanishing Point, and a diplomatic trip by James Taylor.

segments.title: Listener mail: minimum wage proposal
segments.summary: Listener Joe Prohaska of Reno, Nevada proposes setting minimum wage based on what it costs to support a family, or keeping it low as a starting wage. The hosts respond that cost-of-living data is outdated and adults with children also work minimum-wage jobs.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener feedback via Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.
